Sumtu syllables are very frequently preceded by an unstressed syllable, often as part of the system of prefixational morphology. These syllables are described here as minor syllables because they may only contain a short, non-contrastive epenthetic schwa [ə̆] which is not transcribed, even though it necessarily bears a tone. [p. 99, sec. 2.4] ... In phonological representations, full syllables are represented as ‘x’, and minor syllables as ‘.’, thus (. x) represents a sequence of minor + major syllables: an iambic foot with two tones. [p. 100] ... Like many languages in the mainland South-East Asian linguistic area, Sumtu has many words iambic in form, as described in 2.4. Unrestricted major syllables, which may have the form of any permitted syllable in the language, may be preceded by a restricted half-syllable comprising a single initial consonant (most commonly ʔ) and a short epenthetic schwa [ə̆], unmarked in this transcription. [p. 115, sec. 7] ... Iambic feet have a single lexical tone which aligns with the major syllable. The minor syllable is assigned the polar opposite tone, observing the OCP as in Section 9.2 above. Both quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators: printed p.99 (PDF p.3), sec. 2.4 'Morphophonological structure': 'Sumtu syllables are very frequently preceded by an unstressed syllable, often as part of the system of prefixational morphology. These syllables are described here as minor syllables because they may only contain a short, non-contrastive epenthetic schwa [ə̆] which is not transcribed, even though it necessarily bears a tone.'; printed p.115 (PDF p.19), sec. 7 'Tone in iambic feet': 'Like many languages in the mainland South-East Asian linguistic area, Sumtu has many words iambic in form,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sumtu is a tone language: every syllable, major or minor, carries lexical or assigned high or low tone. The only stress statement is structural: words are often sesquisyllabic/iambic, a reduced minor syllable (C + short epenthetic schwa, optionally + m/n) that is explicitly 'unstressed' preceding the full major syllable, which is the prominent syllable and the one the foot's single lexical tone aligns with; the minor syllable receives the polar-opposite tone. Prominence thus falls on the final (major) syllable of the iambic foot; nothing is said about stress placement in words of two full syllables or in longer compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Minor syllables may be lexical (sesquisyllabic nouns) or prefixes (pronominal, transitive -m, non-singular -n); a non-syllabic prefix m- before a stop is not a minor syllable (p.100, ex. 1a, 1e). Tone behaviour (polarity, OCP, dual tone flip) is the paper's focus and has its own complications.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (sesquisyllabic lexemes and prefix+stem words) in a single speaker's Myebon dialect, elicited from a 68-lesson reader read aloud; 'stressed' on p.117 ('Sumtu drops pronouns which are not stressed or in focus') is phrase-level emphasis, not word stress. Author states the segmental phonology is outside the paper's scope.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Myebon-township dialect of Sumtu Chin [csv] sumt1234 as spoken by one elderly speaker (Dong Ling, author of the 2008 Sumtu Reader); Watkins notes tones and vowels differ significantly between Sumtu dialects. Glottolog's cited title is the SOAS WPL 16 working-paper version ('A first look at tone..'); the file held is the peer-reviewed LTBA 36(2) version ('A first account of tone..'), same author and year. Sumtu is closely related to but distinct from Laitu Chin [clj] lait1239 and Songlai Chin [csj] song1313 (both undescribed).

new_statements.quote: Like many languages in the mainland South-East Asian Sprachbund, Sumtu words very often follow an iambic pattern and take the form of sesquisyllables, consisting of an unrestricted major syllable which may have the form of any permitted syllable in the language, preceded by a restricted minor syllable comprising a single initial consonant (most commonly ʔ) and, occasionally, a final nasal m or n. The vowel of the minor syllable is a short epenthetic schwa, which is unmarked in this transcription. [p. 95] | Left-spreading polarity assigns the tone of a lexcially toneless minor syllable to the left of a lexically determined root tone. [p. 102]

new_statements.relation_note: This is the working-paper version of the LTBA 36(2) article that supplies the existing statement (same author, year, data and analysis; retitled 'A first account of tone..' in LTBA). It describes the same iambic minor+major structure with the lexical tone aligned to the major syllable, so it supports the existing 'tone language with a stress statement' reading. One difference in wording: this version does NOT call minor syllables 'unstressed' (that word was added in the LTBA revision, p. 99 sec. 2.4); here the minor syllable is described only as restricted, with a short epenthetic schwa, and the word shape as 'iambic'. Nothing contradicts the catalog.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sumtu is a two-tone language (H vs L, sec. 3, p. 83); every syllable, minor or major, surfaces with a tone. Word-level prominence is described only through word shape: words are very often iambic sesquisyllables, a reduced minor syllable (single consonant, most often glottal stop, with a short untranscribed epenthetic schwa, optionally final m/n) followed by a full major syllable; the lexical tone belongs to the major syllable and the minor syllable receives the polar-opposite tone by left-spreading (sec. 8.4, p. 102). Thus prominence, insofar as the paper describes it, sits on the final (major) syllable of the iambic foot. No statement about stress on words made of full syllables; the word 'stress' appears once, in a phrase-level focus sense: 'Sumtu drops pronouns which are not stressed or in focus' (p. 96).
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tonal exceptions only: 'dual flip-flop' reverses the tones of a sesquisyllable to distinguish dual from plural (sec. 8.5, pp. 102-103), and high-tone verbs exceptionally keep an HH minor+major sequence in the plural (p. 103).
new_statements.identity_note: Both versions describe the Myebon dialect only: the tone data 'is based solely on the Myebon dialect of Dong Ling' (U Daung, aged 75, author of the Sumtu Reader), recorded in Minbya in February 2013 (sec. 1.5, p. 81). Watkins stresses that Sumtu dialects differ markedly in tone and vowels, and that Minbya speakers characterise Myebon speech as 'sing-song', so the description should not be generalised to other Sumtu dialects. This matches the catalog entry name 'Sumtu Chin, Myebon dialect'.
